# Clear Vent

> Dryer vent cleaning company serving Minneapolis, Saint Paul and the Twin Cities suburbs (Hennepin, Ramsey, Dakota, Washington, Anoka, Scott, Carver counties). Flat-rate pricing: $139 for wall/ground-level vents, $199 for roof vents. No trip charge. Online booking at https://clearventmn.com/book. Phone (612) 682-1616.

## Key facts
- Service: full-length rotary brush + HEPA vacuum dryer vent cleaning, exterior cap cleared, transition hose checked, before/after airflow reading, photos.
- Pricing: wall/ground vent $139; roof vent $199; add-ons: Bird nest / animal debris removal $69; Pest-proof vent cover install $89; Dryer interior lint cleanout $49; Replace flexible transition hose $39; Second dryer at same address $89; Camera inspection + photo report $29. Multi-unit from $79/unit.
- Scheduling: usually within 2–4 days; Saturdays available; 2-hour arrival windows; free reschedule with 12 hours notice; pay on completion (card, cash, Zelle, Venmo).
- Recommended frequency: every 12 months; every 6 months for roof vents, heavy use, pets or gas dryers.

## FAQ (119 questions)
https://clearventmn.com/faq
- Q: What is dryer vent cleaning?
  A: Dryer vent cleaning is the removal of lint and debris from the entire duct that runs from the back of your dryer to the vent cap outside your home. We use a rotating brush system and a high-powered vacuum to scrub the full length of the duct, clear the exterior cap, and verify airflow afterward. It is different from cleaning the lint screen, which only catches a portion of the lint your dryer produces.
- Q: How often should a dryer vent be cleaned?
  A: Once a year for most households, and every six months if you do more than 8 loads a week, have pets, own a roof-vented dryer, or have a duct longer than 25 feet. The U.S. Fire Administration and most dryer manufacturers recommend annual cleaning as the baseline.
- Q: Why does lint build up in the vent if I clean the lint trap every load?
  A: The lint screen only catches about 75% of lint. The rest travels down the duct with the hot, moist exhaust air, sticks to the duct walls, and packs tightest at elbows, screens, and the exterior cap. Over a year a typical family's duct collects a few cups to several gallons of lint.
- Q: How long does dryer vent cleaning take?
  A: Most wall or ground-level vents take 45–60 minutes. Roof vents take 60–90 minutes because we clear the cap from the roof and clean the vertical run from both ends. Bird nest removal or a very long duct can add 20–30 minutes.
- Q: Does dryer vent cleaning really make a difference?
  A: Yes. The most common result customers notice is that dry times drop from two cycles back to one. A clean vent restores airflow, lowers the dryer's operating temperature, cuts energy use by up to 30%, extends the life of the heating element and motor, and removes the number one cause of dryer fires.
- Q: What is the difference between dryer vent cleaning and air duct cleaning?
  A: Dryer vent cleaning cleans the single 4-inch exhaust duct from your dryer to the outdoors. Air duct cleaning cleans the HVAC supply and return ductwork for your furnace and AC. They require different tools and we specialize only in dryer vents, so you get a technician who does this all day.
- Q: Do I need to be home for dryer vent cleaning?
  A: Someone 18 or older needs to let us in and move anything blocking the laundry area. After that you don't need to stay in the room. For roof vents we also need access to the yard side where we set up the ladder.
- Q: Can you clean the dryer vent from inside without going outside?
  A: For most wall vents, yes, we clean from inside and verify at the exterior cap. For roof vents we always clear the cap from the roof because that is where the worst clog usually sits; cleaning only from inside can push a lint plug into the cap and make the problem worse.
- Q: Is dryer vent cleaning messy?
  A: No. Our vacuum captures lint as the brush dislodges it, we lay down a drop cloth behind the dryer, and we clean up before we leave. You should not see any lint in the laundry room when we're done.
- Q: Will cleaning damage my dryer or ductwork?
  A: No. We use flexible nylon brushes sized to 4-inch duct that scrub without scratching or dislodging joints. If we find damaged, crushed, or disconnected duct we stop, show you, and tell you what it would cost to fix before touching it.
- Q: What is a dryer vent made of?
  A: Code calls for rigid or semi-rigid aluminum or galvanized steel duct, 4 inches in diameter, with joints taped not screwed. Many homes have white vinyl or foil flex duct instead, which traps lint in its ridges and is a fire hazard. We flag flex duct whenever we find it.
- Q: How much lint comes out of a typical dryer vent?
  A: A vent that hasn't been cleaned in a few years typically yields one to three gallons of packed lint. We have pulled over a 13-gallon bag from a roof vent that had never been cleaned in 15 years.
- Q: Do you clean the dryer itself?
  A: Lint behind the drum and around the heating element is an optional add-on. The standard service covers the duct from the back of the dryer to the outdoor cap, including the flexible transition hose.
- Q: How do I know if my dryer vent is clogged?
  A: The five most common signs are clothes taking more than one cycle to dry, the dryer or laundry room feeling very hot, a burning smell while the dryer runs, lint building up around the outdoor vent cap or behind the dryer, and the outdoor vent flap not opening while the dryer runs.
- Q: Why does my dryer take two cycles to dry clothes?
  A: A restricted vent is the number one cause. When airflow drops, moist air can't leave the drum, so clothes stay damp and the dryer runs longer. If the lint screen is clean and the dryer still takes two cycles, the vent is almost always the culprit.
- Q: Why is the top of my dryer hot to the touch?
  A: Heat that should be exhausting outdoors is backing up because the vent is restricted. A dryer with good airflow stays warm, not hot. This is a safety warning sign, not just an annoyance.
- Q: Why does my laundry room smell like burning when the dryer runs?
  A: Lint sitting on or near the heating element is scorching. Stop using the dryer and book a cleaning. A burning smell is one of the last warnings before a dryer fire.
- Q: Why is there lint on the outside of my house near the vent?
  A: Lint escaping around the cap means the cap, flapper, or screen is partially blocked and exhaust is finding another way out. The inside of the duct is usually worse than what you see.
- Q: My dryer vent flap doesn't open when the dryer runs. What does that mean?
  A: Airflow is too weak to push the flapper open, or the flapper is stuck shut with lint. Either way exhaust is being forced back into the duct. This is a reliable visual test you can do yourself in two minutes.
- Q: Why are my clothes still damp after a full cycle?
  A: Moisture can't leave the drum because exhaust air isn't exiting the house. Clean the lint screen, then run a timed cycle and check the outdoor flap. If airflow is weak, the vent needs cleaning.
- Q: Why is there moisture or condensation in my laundry room?
  A: Humid exhaust is leaking back into the room, often from a disconnected or crushed transition hose behind the dryer or a plugged duct. We reconnect and seal hoses as part of the service.
- Q: Is excessive lint on my lint screen a sign of a clogged vent?
  A: Not directly, but more lint on the screen often means the dryer is running longer cycles because of a restricted vent. Watch dry times rather than screen lint.
- Q: Why did my dryer shut off mid-cycle?
  A: Modern dryers have thermal fuses and high-limit thermostats that trip when the dryer overheats. Overheating is almost always caused by restricted airflow. Many customers call us after a repair tech replaced a thermal fuse and told them to clean the vent.
- Q: My new dryer takes forever to dry. Is the dryer defective?
  A: Usually not. A new dryer connected to an old clogged vent will perform badly from day one. Have the vent cleaned before calling for warranty service; many manufacturers won't cover airflow-related complaints.
- Q: What does a clogged dryer vent look like?
  A: Inside the duct, you see gray felt-like lint coating the walls and packed plugs at elbows. At the exterior cap you see lint hanging from the louvers or matted on a screen. Behind the dryer, lint piles up on the floor if the hose is leaking.
- Q: How much does dryer vent cleaning cost in the Twin Cities?
  A: Our flat rate is $139 for a wall or ground-level vent and $199 for a roof vent, with no trip charge or hidden fees. Most Twin Cities companies charge $100–$250 depending on vent location and add trip fees; we publish our pricing so you know the total before you book.
- Q: Why does a roof dryer vent cost more to clean?
  A: Roof vents require a ladder setup, roof safety gear, clearing the cap from above, and cleaning the vertical run from both ends. It takes longer and carries more risk, so the flat rate is $199 instead of $139.
- Q: Are there any hidden fees or trip charges?
  A: No. The price you see when you book is the price you pay unless you add optional services on site, which we confirm with you first. No trip charge, no fuel surcharge, no weekend upcharge.
- Q: When do I pay?
  A: After the job is done and you're satisfied. We accept credit and debit cards, cash, Zelle, and Venmo. No deposit is required to book.
- Q: Do you offer discounts for multiple dryers or units?
  A: Yes. A second dryer at the same address is $89, and multi-unit buildings start at $79 per unit for scheduled whole-building cleanings. Contact us for a quote on 4 or more units.
- Q: What if you find a bird nest or extra work?
  A: We show you the issue and the add-on price before doing anything extra. Bird nest removal is $69. You can always decline the add-on and we will complete the standard cleaning as booked.
- Q: Is dryer vent cleaning worth the cost?
  A: A clogged vent adds 15–30 minutes to each load, which for a family doing 8 loads a week is roughly $80–$120 a year in extra electricity or gas, plus a shorter dryer lifespan. One cleaning typically pays for itself within the year before you count fire prevention.
- Q: Does homeowners insurance cover dryer vent cleaning?
  A: Routine cleaning is maintenance and is not covered. However, some insurers ask about dryer vent maintenance after a fire claim, and documented annual cleaning can help. We email a receipt with before/after notes you can keep on file.
- Q: Do you charge more for long duct runs?
  A: No. Our flat rate covers duct runs up to 35 feet, which includes nearly every home in the metro. If a run is unusually long or has more than four elbows we tell you before starting, and the price stays within the posted range.
- Q: Can I get a quote without booking?
  A: Yes, but you don't need one. Pricing is flat and listed on the pricing page. If you tell us whether the vent exits through the roof or the wall, you know your exact price.
- Q: Do you price match other dryer vent cleaning companies?
  A: If a licensed, insured local competitor offers a lower written price for the same service, send it over and we will match or beat it.
- Q: How do I know if my dryer vents through the roof?
  A: Look outside for a vent cap near your dryer's side of the house. If there is no 4-inch cap on any exterior wall and your laundry is on an upper floor or an interior wall, look at the roof for a small hooded cap, usually gray or black. During booking we show animated pictures of both so you can pick.
- Q: Why do roof dryer vents clog faster?
  A: Hot moist air has to travel straight up, and lint falls back down when the dryer stops, so lint stacks at the bottom elbow and mats against the cap screen at the top. Roof caps also have a damper or screen that catches lint and is rarely inspected because no one goes on the roof.
- Q: Do you go on the roof to clean the vent?
  A: Yes, when roof pitch and weather allow. We clear the cap, remove any screen or nest, and run the brush down from the top while vacuuming at the dryer. On very steep or icy roofs we clean from inside with an extended rod system and inspect the cap with a camera.
- Q: Can you clean a roof dryer vent in winter?
  A: Yes. We clean from inside the home with an extended brush system and verify flow at the cap. If the roof is safe to walk we clear the cap from above; if it is iced, we schedule a quick free follow-up visit to check the cap when it melts.
